newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia court orders activists be detained longer.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia court orders activists be detained longer.

text.p: A Malaysian court on Wednesday ordered 10 local activists to spend another three days in jail so police could continue investigating the stormy breakup of a conference on East Timor last weekend.
Malaysian police had asked the Magistrates Court to keep the human rights activists in jail another 10 days -- the maximum time they could have asked for without filing formal charges.
Lawyers for the detainees immediately lodged an appeal against the order with the High Court.

After the police vans taking the detainees back to jail got stuck in traffic just outside the Kuala Lumpur city centre police station, families of the detainees rushed to hug their loved ones through the vehicles' windows.

The 10 were among 13 Malaysian activists still in jail after a youth mob allied to the goverment smashed into the Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor II last Saturday, overturning furniture and manhandling participants.
"They (police) want further time to investigate," Haji Sulaiman, a lawyer for the defendants, told reporters outside the courthouse before the court handed down the remand order.
"So they asked for the maximum 10 days."
Under Malaysian law, police can detain people for 14 days before bringing formal charges against them.
"What's there to investigate?," Sulaiman said. "You (police) went in there, you said they refused to disperse, you arrested them. What other information do you need?"
The Kuala Lumpur conference was held ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili.
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year, a move never recognised by the United Nations.
The Malaysian government had objected to the conference, saying it could harm ties with neighbouring Indonesia, but stopped short of banning it.
Some 56 Malaysian activists and journalists have been released from jail this week following the disruption and another 46 foreign participants were deported.
Seven of the youth group demonstrators were detained on Saturday. All were released a few hours later.
Another defence lawyer, Dominic Pondicheary, said he found it strange that police had asked for more time to investigate the 10 after releasing most of the activists earlier this week.
"If they could release 50 people in four days, why do they need another 10 days for 10 people?," Pondicheary said.

The 10 include Kua Kia Soong, a former opposition member of Parliament and a leading human rights activist; Sivarasa Rasiah, a well-known human rights lawyer, and Nasir Hashim, a veteran human rights campaigner and academic.

The Malaysian Bar Council has called for "the immediate and unconditional release of all conference organisers and participants" and for "action to be taken against those who resorted to unlawful action to disrupt the meeting".
